lead: Android is not one program but a fixed stack of layers, from a Linux kernel at the bottom to the dialer and contacts apps at the top. Your own app sits just above the Java API framework. The SDK, the software development kit, is the set of tools that compiles your code and installs it against one chosen version of that stack. Every Android project starts here: pick a platform version, build an APK, push it to a phone or an emulator. This chapter opens the stack, then opens the toolbox.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for what an operating-system layer is and why apps are sandboxed.

sections.h3: The stack, from the kernel up

blocks.text: The Android platform is a stack of six layers. Each layer talks only to the layer directly below it. That single rule keeps a camera bug away from the power driver.

Linux kernel, at the bottom. It carries the device drivers for touchscreen, Wi-Fi, camera and audio, and it does process isolation: every app runs as its own Linux user id, so one app cannot read another app's memory. It also handles power management and kills processes when memory runs low.

HAL, the hardware abstraction layer, sits on the kernel. It is a set of standard C interfaces for camera, audio, sensors and Bluetooth. A phone maker writes one HAL module per chip, and the layer above calls the same function names on every phone. This is why one Android release ships on hardware from many vendors.

Native libraries and the Android runtime share the next layer. The libraries are C and C++ code: SQLite for databases, OpenGL ES for drawing, the WebView engine for web content, which is Chromium-based on modern Android (it used WebKit before Android 4.4), media codecs, and Bionic, Android's own C library. The runtime is ART, the Android Runtime. Your Java or Kotlin source becomes DEX bytecode, a register-based format built for small memory, and ART executes it. ART replaced Dalvik from Android 5.0, compiling ahead of time at install. From Android 7.0 it also compiles just in time while the app runs, and later ahead-of-time compiles follow the recorded hot paths.

Java API framework. These are the classes you write against: Activity for one screen, View for a widget, ContentProvider for shared data, NotificationManager, PackageManager. Chapter 2.4 and Unit 3 use them; here you only need to know they form a thin layer over everything below.
System apps at the top: dialer, contacts, messages, settings, launcher. They are ordinary apps on the same framework API, which is why you can install a replacement launcher.

sections.h3: The SDK: what is inside the box

blocks.text: The SDK is not one program. It is a folder of tools, libraries and platform files that the SDK Manager downloads into versioned subfolders. Android Studio is an editor and debugger standing in front of it. Without the SDK, Studio opens your files but cannot build.

items: Platforms: one folder per API level, for example platforms/android-34. Inside is android.jar, the compiled framework classes your code is checked against.
Build-tools: versioned programs that run during a build. AAPT2 compiles XML resources and generates the R class; d8 converts Java bytecode into DEX.
Platform-tools: adb, the Android Debug Bridge, plus fastboot. adb install puts an APK on a phone, adb logcat prints the log, adb shell gives a shell on the device.
Emulator and system images: a complete Android image per API level. An AVD, Android Virtual Device, is a named setup of image, screen size and RAM that the emulator boots.
Command-line tools: sdkmanager and avdmanager, for build servers where nobody clicks a mouse.

blocks.text: Gradle is the build system. The Android Gradle Plugin adds tasks such as assembleDebug, which writes app-debug.apk. Logcat is one shared log stream carrying lines from every app and from the framework. Lint reads your source and resources for likely bugs before you run anything.

sections.h3: API level and the three numbers

blocks.text: An API level is the integer that names a platform version. Android 5.0 is API 21, Android 7.0 is API 24, Android 8.0 is API 26, Android 14 is API 34. Code and documentation use the integer because the marketing name changes every year.
compileSdk is the platform folder used at build time. It fixes which framework classes and methods type-check: a class added in API 35 fails to compile under compileSdk 34.
minSdk is the lowest API level allowed to install the APK. The package manager reads it from the manifest and refuses anything lower.

targetSdk is the level you tested against and whose behaviour changes you accept. Android keeps old behaviour switched on for apps with a lower targetSdk, a compatibility mode. Raising targetSdk turns those switches off: background execution limits from API 26, stricter background location rules later.

minSdk and targetSdk are written in the module's build.gradle, and Gradle copies them into the manifest as minSdkVersion and targetSdkVersion. compileSdk is build-time only and is never put in the manifest.

examples.question: A module's build.gradle sets compileSdk 34, minSdk 24 and targetSdk 34. A tester's phone reports API level 21. Explain what each of the three numbers means for this build, and state exactly what the tester sees when the APK is installed.
steps: compileSdk 34: the build compiles against platforms/android-34/android.jar. Any call into the Android 14 framework type-checks; a call to a class added in API 35 stops the build with a cannot-find-symbol error.
minSdk 24: Gradle writes minSdkVersion 24 into the APK manifest. At install time the package manager compares the phone's API level with 24.
The phone reports 21. Since 21 < 24, installation is refused with INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK, and on Google Play the listing is filtered out, so the app does not appear in search on that phone.
targetSdk 34: on a phone at API 34 or higher the app runs with Android 14 behaviour, because the compatibility switches kept for older targets stay off.

To support the tester, drop minSdk to 21. compileSdk stays at 34, and each call to a method added after API 21 must be wrapped in a guard using that method's own API level, for example if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26) for a method added in API 26. Without the guard the app compiles and then throws NoSuchMethodError on the API 21 phone.
examples.answer: compileSdk 34 fixes the compile-time framework and targetSdk 34 opts the app into Android 14 behaviour, while minSdk 24 blocks the API 21 tester, who is 3 API levels short and sees INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK plus no Play Store listing.

traps: Swapping compileSdk and targetSdk. compileSdk is build-time only; targetSdk is a run-time behaviour opt-in, and reversing them is the examiner's favourite mistake.
Thinking Android Studio is the SDK. Studio is the editor; the SDK is the platforms, build-tools and platform-tools folders it drives.
Lowering minSdk as if it were free. Each call to a newer API then needs a Build.VERSION.SDK_INT guard, or the app crashes with NoSuchMethodError on old phones.
Reading API level as the Android version number. API 21 is Android 5.0, not Android 21.
Placing ART above the native libraries. ART is the runtime that executes DEX and sits beside them, not on top of them.

quiz.q: Name the six layers of the Android platform, from top to bottom.
quiz.a: System apps, Java API framework, native libraries, Android runtime, HAL, Linux kernel.

quiz.q: What is an API level? Give two mappings between an integer and an Android version.
quiz.a: An integer naming a platform version: API 21 is Android 5.0, API 34 is Android 14.

quiz.q: Why does Android need a HAL instead of letting the framework call drivers directly?
quiz.a: The HAL gives one fixed set of C interfaces per device class, so the framework calls the same names on every vendor's hardware; the phone maker supplies a chip-specific module underneath and the framework never changes.

quiz.q: Which SDK component do you use to (a) read log output from a connected phone, (b) compile XML resources?
quiz.a: (a) adb logcat, from platform-tools. (b) AAPT2, from build-tools, which also generates the R class.

quiz.q: An app has compileSdk 34, minSdk 26, targetSdk 33 and is installed on a phone at API 34. Does it get Android 14 behaviour or Android 13 behaviour? Why?
quiz.a: Android 13 behaviour. Behaviour switches follow targetSdk, and targetSdk 33 means the Android 14 changes stay off even though the device itself is at API 34.

quiz.q: minSdk is 21 and the code calls a method added in API 26 with no guard. What happens on an API 23 phone?
quiz.a: The APK installs, because 23 ≥ 21. The call is resolved at run time on ART, finds no such method, and throws NoSuchMethodError, so the app crashes when that line runs.

quiz.q: The same APK is installed on an API 29 phone and an API 33 phone, with targetSdk 31. Explain why behaviour can still differ, and where targetSdk stops mattering.
quiz.a: Each phone applies behaviour changes up to the lower of its own API level and targetSdk. The API 29 phone only has changes up to 29 available; the API 33 phone applies changes up to 31, and skips the API 32 and 33 changes because targetSdk 31 keeps those compatibility switches on. Above targetSdk, the targetSdk number stops mattering.

quiz.q: Why do app stores require a recent targetSdk for new listings?
quiz.a: A low targetSdk lets an app keep old compatibility behaviour forever, including looser background and privacy rules. Requiring a recent value forces developers to test and accept newer behaviour, so security and battery fixes actually reach users.

beyond: Not for the exam. Project Treble split the HAL from the framework so a phone can receive a new Android version without the chip vendor rewriting every driver. Mainline modules now update core framework pieces through the store, like ordinary apps. ART keeps improving through baseline profiles, which list the hot code paths and ship inside the APK so ART can compile them ahead of time at install, making start-up faster. Search for Project Treble, ART baseline profiles, and the Android Gradle Plugin release notes to follow where this layer is heading.
